title: Protectionism
examples: What is the difference between a tariff and a quota?
Can you give an example of a country using protectionism?

explain.say: Today we will explore protectionism in economics. Say what protectionism means in your own words.
First we look at tariffs. Say a tariff is a tax on imported goods. This tax makes foreign products more expensive here.
Next we study quotas. Say a quota is a direct limit on the quantity of imports. It sets a maximum amount allowed.
So we compare tariffs and quotas. Say a tariff raises the price by tax. A quota restricts the actual amount you can buy.

draw.text: Tariff vs Quota: Tax vs Limit

explain.say: Arguments for protectionism exist. Say governments might use it to protect new local industries. This helps them grow bigger.
In real life, say a country might tax imported steel. This helps local steel factories keep workers employed. This is a common economic tool.

faq.q: What is the main difference between a tariff and a quota?
faq.a: A tariff is a tax applied to imports, which raises the price. A quota is a physical limit on the number of goods that can be imported.
asks: Are they both ways to limit trade?
Does a tax or a limit affect the market more?

faq.q: Why would a government want to use protectionism?
faq.a: Governments often use it to protect young, local industries from strong foreign competition. They argue this helps the economy develop.
asks: Is it always good for the economy?
What is the goal of protecting local jobs?

faq.a: Often, yes. By limiting choice or raising prices through taxes, consumers might end up paying more for less variety.
asks: Will my wallet suffer from tariffs?
Is it better for consumers to have free trade?

faq.q: Can a country use both tariffs and quotas at the same time?
faq.a: Yes, a country could impose both measures simultaneously. This would create a very strong barrier to foreign trade.
asks: Can a country use multiple trade restrictions?

faq.q: What is the argument against protectionism?
faq.a: The main argument is that it slows down economic growth. Free trade allows countries to specialize and benefit from global efficiency.
asks: What is the downside of trade barriers?

facts: Tariffs are taxes levied on goods crossing a country's border.
A quota sets an absolute maximum physical limit on imports.
Proponents argue protectionism helps 'infant industries' mature.
Critics argue protectionism leads to higher consumer prices and less choice.

quiz.say: A government places a direct cap on the number of imported cars allowed next year. This action is an example of a:
quiz.show: Tariff or Quota? Cap on goods?
quiz.why: A quota sets a maximum quantity, which is a direct limit on the number of items.

wrong.0: A subsidy is money given to encourage production, the opposite of restriction.
wrong.1: Taxation is a general term; a tariff is the specific tax on imports.
wrong.3: A tariff is a tax, not a physical limit on the number of cars.

quiz.say: If a country imposes a tax on imported electronics, what economic tool is it using?
quiz.why: A tax placed on imported goods is specifically called a tariff.

wrong.0: A quota limits the quantity, it does not involve adding a tax.
wrong.1: A subsidy helps domestic producers, it does not tax imports.
wrong.2: This is a description, not the name of the tool itself.

quiz.say: Which statement best describes the argument for protectionism?

options.show: To lower the cost of all goods.
options.say: To lower the cost of all goods.

options.show: To shield new local industries from foreign competition.
options.say: To shield new local industries from foreign competition.

quiz.why: The primary argument is protecting 'infant industries' until they are large enough.

wrong.0: Taxes like tariffs generally increase the final cost for consumers.
wrong.1: Protectionism goes against the principle of global specialization.
wrong.3: Protectionism usually restricts choice by limiting imports.
